concept.technique_name: modular remainder of a power (congruence reduction)

examples.problem_statement: The first two, 2 digit numbers that divide (21^(12346)-1) are?

solution.description: Test the smallest two-digit divisor, 10, by replacing 21 with the remainder it leaves on division by 10, namely 1, so the power becomes 1^{12346}.
Evaluate that reduced expression: 1 raised to any power is 1, and subtracting 1 leaves remainder 0, which confirms 10 is a divisor.
Test the next two-digit number, 11, by replacing 21 with -1, since 21 is one more than the multiple 22, so the power becomes (-1)^{12346}.
Evaluate that expression: the exponent 12346 is even so (-1)^{12346} = 1, and subtracting 1 leaves remainder 0, confirming 11 is also a divisor.
Collect the two smallest two-digit numbers that were shown to leave remainder 0, taking them in increasing order as the answer.

key_reminders: A power can be reduced modulo n by first replacing the base with its remainder modulo n.
21 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}, and (-1) raised to an even power equals 1.
a^k - 1 is divisible by n exactly when a^k leaves remainder 1 modulo n.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that the exponent 12346 is even, and taking (-1)^{12346} = -1 instead of 1 for the modulo-11 test.
Starting the search at 11 and overlooking 10, which is the smaller two-digit divisor.

concept.technique_name: overlapping sets formula with extreme-value bounds

examples.problem_statement: Of 320 consumers, 200 eat strawberries and 300 eat oranges. How many people could eat both fruits? Select all that apply. Choices: 140, 150, 170, 180, 190, 210.

solution.description: Set up the two-set overlap formula with the given totals; note that it contains two unknowns, Both and Neither, so a single value cannot be pinned down yet.

solution.result: at least 300 of the 320 eat some fruit
solution.description: Look for a hidden constraint: because 300 people eat oranges, at least 300 people must eat some kind of fruit, which limits how large Neither can be.
Count the people not covered by the orange group: only these 20 could possibly eat no fruit at all, so Neither runs from 0 up to 20.
Substitute the two endpoints of the Neither range back into the formula to get the minimum overlap of 180 and the maximum overlap of 200.
Scan the answer choices and keep every value lying between the two bounds, since any value in that range is achievable.

key_reminders: Total = Group 1 + Group 2 - Both + Neither for two overlapping sets.
The overlap is minimized when Neither is smallest and maximized when Neither is largest.
In a select-all question every value inside the valid range must be chosen, not just the endpoint.
common_mistakes: Reporting only the minimum 180 and missing 190, which also lies inside the achievable range.
Assuming Neither must be 0, which fixes Both at exactly 180 and hides the upper bound of 200.

concept.technique_name: fraction of a fraction, then complement from 1

examples.problem_statement: 1/5 of all the cars on a certain auto lot are red, and 2/3 of all the red cars are convertibles. What fraction of all the cars are NOT red convertibles?

solution.description: Recognize that the convertible fraction applies to the red cars only, so a fraction of a fraction is found by multiplying the two fractions.

solution.result: \frac{2}{15} \text{ of all cars are red convertibles}
solution.description: Carry out that multiplication across numerators and denominators to get the share of the whole lot that is both red and a convertible.
Because the question asks for the cars that are NOT red convertibles, subtract the part just found from the whole lot, represented by 1.

key_reminders: "A fraction of a fraction" means multiply the two fractions.
The second fraction is taken of the red cars, not of all the cars.
A NOT question is answered by subtracting the computed part from 1.
common_mistakes: Adding 1/5 and 2/3 instead of multiplying them, which treats the two groups as separate rather than nested.
Stopping at 2/15 and reporting the red convertibles instead of the complement 13/15.

concept.technique_name: least common multiple by listing multiples and by prime factorization

examples.problem_statement: On a radio tower, a red light flashes every 6 seconds and a blue light flashes every 10 seconds. If both lights flash together at a certain time, how many seconds later will both lights flash together the next time?

solution.result: the multiples of 6 measured in seconds after the shared flash
solution.description: List the times the red light flashes, counting seconds forward from the moment both lights flashed together.

solution.result: the multiples of 10 measured in seconds after the shared flash
solution.description: List the blue light's flash times on the same time axis so the two lists can be compared entry by entry.
Scan the two lists for the earliest number appearing in both, since that is the first moment the two lights flash at the same instant again.
Check the same answer the faster way by writing each interval as a product of primes and taking 2 once with the unshared factors 3 and 5 to build the least common multiple.

key_reminders: The next simultaneous flash occurs at the least common multiple of the two intervals.
For the LCM by prime factorization, a prime shared by both numbers is counted once, not twice.
common_mistakes: Multiplying 6 by 10 to get 60, which double-counts the shared factor 2 and gives the second simultaneous flash rather than the first.
Taking the greatest common factor 2 instead of the least common multiple.
